newsitem.title: FRANCE: Zeroual to break silence, amid unremitting bloodshed.
newsitem.headline: Zeroual to break silence, amid unremitting bloodshed.

text.p: After days of little official comment as bombs and attacks killed nearly 200 people in and around his capital, Algerian President Liamine Zeroual is to address the country on television late on Friday (1900 GMT).
Diplomatic sources in Algiers expect him to speak either of the intensified killings, which the authorities blame on Moslem fundamentalists, or on a promised general election, or both.
"Zeroual sees elections as a way out of the violence, but the GIA (Armed Islamic Group) has promised its war will go on whatever happens," one of the sources said on Friday.
At least five bombs have hit Algiers, home to three to four million people, in the past week. Another 17 have been defused, while others exploded in nearby towns.
The killings and maiming of scores of people have spread fear and suspicion, and brought harsh criticism of a repeated government statement that only 'residual terrorism' remained.

"The last public statement about a week ago said the state would do its utmost to vanquish terrorism," said one political commentator on Friday, pointing out that the authorities had now dropped their stand on 'residual terrorism' which had been condemned even by members of the official quasi-parliament.

Algiers residents said on Friday that six more people had been killed in the past two nights and that an unconfirmed report circulating in the city said 22 had died, their throats cut, in Benhamdane, Blida province, during Wednesday night.

"No indication has filtered out on the details of his (Zeroual's) speech," Algerian radio said, but added that a special meeting of the unelected National Transitional Council (CNT) would be held on Saturday.
The CNT has been looking at two new laws, one on political parties which particularly bans those based on religion, and one on a system of proportional representation for the poll.
The CNT was set up months after the elected parliament was dissolved by outgoing president Chadli Benjedid early in 1992.
Shortly after, the authorities scrapped an election which the now banned Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) was poised to win.

Around a dozen CNT members have been killed by suspected fundamentalists. An official from another government-appointed body, the council for Algiers suburb of Badjarrah, was the latest victim to die, residents said on Friday.
A deputy major, he was shot at about 8 p.m. on Thursday.
Algeria's authorities early in the conflict abolished councils dominated by FIS elected members and replaced them. Scores of these appointed officials have also been killed.

State radio said on Friday Zeroual will soon start talks with political parties ahead of elections, seen as a way of bringing the country's 29 million people out of five years of bloodshed. About 60,000 people have died.
But he wants new rules for the poll he has promised in the first half of 1997, with regional elections also this year.
The government-run newspaper El Moudjahid said early this month that the general election would be held in May.
"It's likely to be May 29, with a second round on June 5," one political commentator in Algiers said on Friday.

Diplomats have said Zeroual is determined to ensure there is no repeat of an Islamists' ballot victory. Some believe an election will do little to change events in Algeria other than to give greater legitimacy abroad to the authorities.

"When we had the presidential election, then the referendum on the constitution last year, people expected change. There has been little. I can't see elections altering anything quickly," one diplomatic source said earlier this week.
